title: What forgiveness isn't
hookLine: forgiving isn't excusing, forgetting, or staying in danger: Luke 17, Joseph, and David at the stronghold

cards: "Just forgive and forget." It gets said in kitchens, over the phone, sometimes to people who are still being hurt. It sounds biblical.
It isn't. Those words aren't in the Bible. And when you read what the Bible does say about forgiving, it turns out to be harder than that slogan in one way, and much safer in another.
This path met forgiveness early, with a servant who wouldn't pass the mercy on. Today, a short list of what it isn't. It isn't excusing.
It isn't forgetting. And it isn't staying in danger.

teach.b: First, it isn't excusing. Jesus says in Luke: "If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him." The wrong gets named first.
Excusing says it wasn't really wrong. Forgiving says it was, and then lets something go.

teach.h: APHIEMI: LET GO OF THE DEBT.
teach.b: The Greek word behind forgive here is aphiemi, and it means to let go, to release, to send away. It's what you do with a debt. You release the claim, the right to get even.
Second, it isn't forgetting. At the end of Genesis, Joseph forgives the brothers who sold him into slavery, and he says it plainly: "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good."
He remembers exactly what they did. He forgives with the memory wide open. Third, it isn't staying in danger.
In First Samuel, King Saul is hunting David to kill him. David has a chance to kill Saul in a cave, and spares him. Saul weeps and admits David is more righteous than he is.
Then the story says Saul goes home, and David and his men go up to the stronghold. David doesn't move back into the palace. He leaves the judging to God, and he keeps his distance.
Forgiveness and trust are different things. Trust may come back slowly, or not at all.
If someone is hurting you, getting safe is not a failure to forgive; if you're in danger, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

how: Christians pray "forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" in the Lord's Prayer, and pastors and Christian counselors teach that forgiving a wrong does not require excusing it, forgetting it, or remaining in an unsafe relationship.

games.q: you're David. you've spared King Saul's life in a cave, and Saul has wept and called you more righteous than himself. now he's heading home. what do you do?
o: go home with him to the palace; it's all forgiven.
go up to the stronghold with your men.
follow him until he apologizes properly.
games.why: Saul goes home, and David and his men go up to the stronghold. he spares his enemy and leaves the judging to God, but he doesn't walk back into danger either.

practice: Bring to mind someone who hurt you, not the deepest wound, something middle-sized, and name what they did, plainly, to yourself.

Then notice the debt, the wish for them to pay, and see if you can set it down, even partway, while keeping whatever boundary keeps you safe; if this stirs up something heavy, stop, and talk with someone you trust.
If you pray, you can use the line from the Lord's Prayer: "forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors."

wordCard.voice: What forgiveness isn't. Not calling a wrong right, not erasing the memory, not walking back into harm. It's letting go of the debt.

orig.note: Greek: to let go, release, send away; a common New Testament word for forgiving a debt or a wrong.

carryVoice: Your line: forgive and stay safe. Forgiveness and trust are different things. Go gently today.
